rv.q: Served wonderfully by its cast, this is a thrilling, meticulous reproach against a society desperate to reconnect with its past, even as it drifts inexorably away.

It is important not to reveal the nature of this twist. Still, it spoils nothing to say that Crowe is looking at subjects that have long interested her: group coercion and the effect that modern technology has on affections, time and concentration.
All the various threads of Crowe's ambition don't quite tie up; the overall conceit amounts to less than it promises
The Sewing Group is insightful about the difficulties of writing a history play...
Crowe is a master of form – but sometimes it crowds out her writing, trapping her play rather than setting it free.
The evening’s virtue lies in its revelations, its vices lie in the handiwork that brings them to the fore.
Her intellectual grasp of our fraying social and psychological fabric is admirable. But the drama is lamentably threadbare.
It's an unendingly fascinating topic expertly explored by Crowe and director/designer Stewart Laing.
The only disappointment is that if the first half is enigmatic, the second – after the play’s big reveal – is too didactic, spelling out its message with increasing shrillness.
The needle-workers keep using modernisms like 'soul mate', 'gluten-free' and 'love interest'.
With nods to Westworld, it remains an intriguing experience, if a slightly frustrating one.
The laborious artiness of the short, self-consciously cryptic scenes that make up large swaths of the play start to chafe pretty early on.
But, after its well-prepared revelations, the 85-minute play becomes a bit fuzzy and loses focus towards the end, and it finally feels a bit flabby when its story begs to have been tighter.

cn.t: Crowe's shape-shifting play divides critics with its provocative structure and uncertain premise about a pre-industrial sewing group. Some find it dazzling and unpredictable; others consider it irritating and overly teasing.
